catalog_quote: Word level stress assignment is not predictable from syllable structure. Rather, stress falls on syllables with H tone. If a word lacks an H tone, stress falls on the first syllable by default. The following three tables illustrate words with similar syllable structures and distinct stress patterns: Table 13 Stress assignment for 2 syllable words. First syllable: ˈkə. ra dog, ˈmá. gan squirrel, ˈʃím. but hair, ˈʒi. ʒjax soup; Second syllable: za. ˈbə́n guinea fowl, ta. ˈkúr chicken, ɣa. ˈláj long ago, bə. ˈlám baboon. Table 14 Stress assignment for 3 syllable words. First Syllable: ˈmá. pa. ram gate, ˈxán. dʒi. ga now, ˈdə́. gə. vu hyena, ˈmá. za. ɣar bat; Final Syllable: ta. pə. ˈʃám calabash, kə. xə. ˈrán dry season, ɓə. la. ˈmá say (count), ji. gə. ˈɮá axe; Medial Syllable: gats. ˈxá. ra lizard, male, rwa. ˈɬí. ɗi prince. Table 15 Stress assignment for words of more than 3 syllables: ˈgə́. ɮəm. bə. la large, undivided calabash; ˌma. ⁿgu. ra. ta. ˈtán army ants. [p. 57-58; table columns linearized] ... Sakun has two tones; high (H) and low (L). Tone is important for both the lexicon and grammar. Tone is phonemic in Sakun, distinguishing words whose segmental structure is otherwise identical. [p. 54]

Tables 13-15 (p.57-58) contain every form the first reader cites (ˈkə.ra 'dog', ˈmá.gan 'squirrel', za.ˈbə́n 'guinea fowl', ta.ˈkúr 'chicken', ˈmá.pa.ram 'gate', ta.pə.ˈʃám 'calabash', gats.ˈxá…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sakun is a two-tone (H/L) language; word stress is tone-driven, not position- or weight-driven: the H-toned syllable carries stress (initial, medial or final depending on where H sits), and words with no H tone get default initial stress. Certain suffixes/clitics (phrase-final determiner =ju, plural -xa, derivational -n) pull stress to the final syllable, -n even overriding a root H tone; sentence intonation overrides word stress where they conflict.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed explicitly; one transcription in Table 15 marks secondary stress on the initial syllable of a 5-syllable word with final H-tone primary stress (ˌma.ⁿgu.ra.ta.ˈtán 'army ants').
new_statements.exceptions: 6.1.1: phrase-final determiner =ju and plural -xa(=j) shift stress to the final syllable of H-less words (ˈlə.bət vs lə.ˈbət.tju; ˈma.pa.ram vs ma.pa.ˈram.xáj); derivational -n takes primary stress even against a competing root H (ˈⁿdás vs mə.ⁿdá.ˈsə́n); suppletive SG/PL 'husband' ˈma.ɮax vs ma.ɮi.ˈxə́. 6.1.2: stress falls on the left edge of the subject NP even without H tone. 6.2: sentence-level intonation trumps word stress at points of conflict (e.g. sentence-final H words in negation get low F0). No statement on which syllable wins when a word has more than one H tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly 'word level stress'; examples are citation forms syllabified with IPA stress marks; separate subsections treat morphologically conditioned shifts, subject-NP (phrasal) stress and sentence intonation overriding word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Thomas describes Sakun as spoken in Sukur (Madagali LGA, Adamawa State); 'Sakun' is the autonym, 'Sukur' the exonym -- same language as Glottolog suku1272 / ISO syk, no dialect restriction stated for the phonology chapter.
